<form class="book-practice" id="quiz-p02" data-practice-set="P02" novalidate>
<p id="quiz-p02-instructions">Choose one answer for each of the 10 questions. Complete the set, then select <strong>Check answers</strong> to see your score and explanations. Each question is worth one point.</p>
<noscript><p>For a self-check without JavaScript, record your choices, then open the answer key below.</p></noscript>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-01" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">1.</span> An estimate starts near an arbitrary number supplied by an interviewer. Separately, a risk estimate rises because a dramatic example comes easily to mind. Which pair fits, in order?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-01-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-01-a" name="p02-01" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Availability; anchoring</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-01-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-01-b" name="p02-01" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Anchoring; availability</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-01-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-01-c" name="p02-01" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Priming; regression to the mean</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-01-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-01-d" name="p02-01" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Halo; conjunction fallacy</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-01-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-01-e" name="p02-01" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Framing; overplacement</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-01-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-02" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">2.</span> A report changes “8% failures” to “92% successes” for the same binary outcome. Another task presents cooking words before an ambiguous word. Which processes are manipulated, respectively?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-02-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-02-a" name="p02-02" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Defaults and anchoring</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-02-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-02-b" name="p02-02" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Semantic priming and framing</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-02-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-02-c" name="p02-02" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Framing and semantic priming</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-02-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-02-d" name="p02-02" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Loss aversion and overprecision</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-02-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-02-e" name="p02-02" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Mere exposure and a conjunction error</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-02-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-03" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">3.</span> A policy slogan claiming that a reform cuts waiting times is easy to process and repeated often. Its supporters accept it without checking the evidence. Which procedure most directly tests its accuracy?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-03-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-03-a" name="p02-03" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> State a falsifiable prediction and examine independent outcome data.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-03-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-03-b" name="p02-03" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare how much the two sides like their slogans.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-03-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-03-c" name="p02-03" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Use a harder font to make the slogan feel less familiar.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-03-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-03-d" name="p02-03" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Ask supporters how natural it sounds.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-03-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-03-e" name="p02-03" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Repeat it to a larger group and count recognition.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-03-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-04" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">4.</span> A recruitment panel wants to prevent an engaging interview from dominating unrelated skill judgments. Which scoring procedure best targets this problem?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-04-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-04-a" name="p02-04" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Average repeated overall-impression ratings collected during the same interview.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-04-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-04-b" name="p02-04" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Give each interviewer an equal vote on the candidate&#x27;s overall impression.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-04-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-04-c" name="p02-04" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Require a longer explanation of the overall impression before scoring dimensions.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-04-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-04-d" name="p02-04" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Rate job-relevant dimensions separately before recording an overall impression.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-04-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-04-e" name="p02-04" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Record an overall impression first and use it to guide dimension ratings.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-04-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-05" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">5.</span> Every application has a final outcome recorded as either success or failure. A report says 3% fail. Its complementary frame must describe the same applications and period. Which statement qualifies?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-05-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-05-a" name="p02-05" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> 3% of accepted applicants later fail.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-05-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-05-b" name="p02-05" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> 97% of those applications succeed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-05-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-05-c" name="p02-05" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> 97 applications succeed.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-05-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-05-d" name="p02-05" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> 3% fewer applications fail than last year.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-05-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-05-e" name="p02-05" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> 97% of rejected applicants would succeed elsewhere.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-05-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-06" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">6.</span> A trader says a new ritual improves forecasting accuracy. Which test most directly estimates its causal effect on comparable forecasting tasks?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-06-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-06-a" name="p02-06" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Ask successful traders whether they remember using the ritual.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-06-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-06-b" name="p02-06" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare confidence before and after performing the ritual.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-06-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-06-c" name="p02-06" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Randomly assign ritual and no-ritual trials, then score all forecasts.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-06-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-06-d" name="p02-06" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Compare voluntary ritual users with people who decline it.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-06-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-06-e" name="p02-06" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Compare forecasts before and after the ritual began.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-06-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-07" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">7.</span> An applicant resembles a successful engineer. A selection test was validated on experienced engineers, but the current applicant pool consists of novices with a different base rate. What should a probability estimate use?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-07-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-07-a" name="p02-07" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> The test&#x27;s sensitivity as the probability of success after passing.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-07-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-07-b" name="p02-07" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Equal prior probabilities because the applicant is unfamiliar.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-07-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-07-c" name="p02-07" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> A justified novice reference class and test performance relevant to that class.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-07-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-07-d" name="p02-07" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> The number of favorable adjectives in the applicant&#x27;s description.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-07-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-07-e" name="p02-07" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> The engineer base rate because the applicant matches the prototype.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-07-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-08" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">8.</span> The lowest-scoring branches receive coaching and improve next month. Which comparison best tests whether coaching contributed beyond regression to the mean?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-08-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-08-a" name="p02-08" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Attribute every gain after coaching to the intervention.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-08-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-08-b" name="p02-08" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Compare only each coached branch with its own worst month.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-08-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-08-c" name="p02-08" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Compare coached low scorers with the highest-scoring branches.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-08-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-08-d" name="p02-08" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Ask coaches to select only branches that later improved.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-08-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-08-e" name="p02-08" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Randomly assign similarly low-scoring branches to coaching or control.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-08-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-09" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">9.</span> A project succeeds if at least one of two independent components works. Each component works with probability 0.8. Which pair gives equivalent success and failure descriptions for the project?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-09-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-09-a" name="p02-09" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> 80% success and 20% failure</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-09-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-09-b" name="p02-09" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> 64% success and 36% failure</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-09-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-09-c" name="p02-09" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> 40% success and 60% failure</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-09-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-09-d" name="p02-09" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> 100% success and 0% failure</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-09-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-09-e" name="p02-09" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> 96% success and 4% failure</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-09-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<fieldset class="practice-question" id="p02-10" aria-describedby="quiz-p02-instructions">
<legend><span class="practice-number">10.</span> Across 200 resolved events, A assigned 20% to 100 events, of which 20 occurred, and 80% to 100 events, of which 80 occurred. B assigned 50% to all 200. What does this record show?</legend>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-10-a"><input type="radio" id="p02-10-a" name="p02-10" value="0"><span><strong>A.</strong> Both are calibrated; B has greater resolution.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-10-b"><input type="radio" id="p02-10-b" name="p02-10" value="1"><span><strong>B.</strong> Only B is calibrated; A has greater resolution.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-10-c"><input type="radio" id="p02-10-c" name="p02-10" value="2"><span><strong>C.</strong> Neither is calibrated; both have equal resolution.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-10-d"><input type="radio" id="p02-10-d" name="p02-10" value="3"><span><strong>D.</strong> Both are calibrated on this record; A has greater resolution.</span></label>
<label class="practice-option" for="p02-10-e"><input type="radio" id="p02-10-e" name="p02-10" value="4"><span><strong>E.</strong> Only A is calibrated; both have equal resolution.</span></label>
<p class="practice-item-result" id="p02-10-result" hidden></p></fieldset>
<div class="practice-controls"><p class="practice-progress" aria-live="polite">0 of 10 answered</p>
<button class="practice-submit" type="submit" disabled>Check answers</button>
<button class="practice-retry" type="button" hidden>Try again</button></div>

<details class="practice-key" id="answers-p02"><summary>Answers and explanations</summary><ol class="practice-answer-list">
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p02-01"><h3>Question 1: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Availability; anchoring <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses the mechanisms.</dd>
<dt>B. Anchoring; availability <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The first uses a numerical starting point; the second uses ease of recall.</dd>
<dt>C. Priming; regression to the mean <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The second is not a repeated extreme measurement.</dd>
<dt>D. Halo; conjunction fallacy <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Neither a global impression nor a probability conjunction is described.</dd>
<dt>E. Framing; overplacement <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No equivalent descriptions or ranking of personal ability is specified.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/09-availability-affect-and-representativeness.html">Chapter 9</a> · <a href="../chapters/11-anchors-halos-and-decoys.html">Chapter 11</a>. <a href="#p02-01">Back to question 1</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p02-02"><h3>Question 2: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Defaults and anchoring <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>No preselected option or initial numerical estimate is manipulated.</dd>
<dt>B. Semantic priming and framing <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses the described manipulations.</dd>
<dt>C. Framing and semantic priming <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>The first changes equivalent description; the second changes concept accessibility.</dd>
<dt>D. Loss aversion and overprecision <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Neither outcome demonstrates these particular judgment patterns.</dd>
<dt>E. Mere exposure and a conjunction error <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Repetition-based liking and intersecting probabilities are not the tasks.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/12-framing.html">Chapter 12</a> · <a href="../chapters/13-priming-fluency-and-familiarity.html">Chapter 13</a>. <a href="#p02-02">Back to question 2</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="0" data-question="p02-03"><h3>Question 3: A</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. State a falsifiable prediction and examine independent outcome data. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>This replaces fluency and repetition with an evidential test.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare how much the two sides like their slogans. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Liking is not a test of the claim.</dd>
<dt>C. Use a harder font to make the slogan feel less familiar. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Lower fluency does not itself establish falsity or truth.</dd>
<dt>D. Ask supporters how natural it sounds. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Naturalness is another fluency judgment.</dd>
<dt>E. Repeat it to a larger group and count recognition. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Recognition measures exposure, not accuracy.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/10-confirmation-bias-and-motivated-reasoning.html">Chapter 10</a> · <a href="../chapters/13-priming-fluency-and-familiarity.html">Chapter 13</a>. <a href="#p02-03">Back to question 3</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p02-04"><h3>Question 4: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Average repeated overall-impression ratings collected during the same interview. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Averaging global ratings does not isolate evidence for distinct skills.</dd>
<dt>B. Give each interviewer an equal vote on the candidate&#x27;s overall impression. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Equal voting weights do not address each evaluator&#x27;s halo effect.</dd>
<dt>C. Require a longer explanation of the overall impression before scoring dimensions. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Elaborating the impression may reinforce rather than separate it.</dd>
<dt>D. Rate job-relevant dimensions separately before recording an overall impression. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Separate initial ratings constrain spillover from a global evaluation.</dd>
<dt>E. Record an overall impression first and use it to guide dimension ratings. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The global judgment may shape each later assessment.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.html">Chapter 8</a> · <a href="../chapters/11-anchors-halos-and-decoys.html">Chapter 11</a>. <a href="#p02-04">Back to question 4</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="1" data-question="p02-05"><h3>Question 5: B</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. 3% of accepted applicants later fail. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This uses a new conditional denominator and outcome.</dd>
<dt>B. 97% of those applications succeed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Success complements failure within the specified population.</dd>
<dt>C. 97 applications succeed. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A count needs the total number of applications to express the same rate.</dd>
<dt>D. 3% fewer applications fail than last year. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This introduces a comparison over time absent from the original.</dd>
<dt>E. 97% of rejected applicants would succeed elsewhere. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This changes both the population and the outcome.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/12-framing.html">Chapter 12</a> · <a href="../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.html">Chapter 14</a>. <a href="#p02-05">Back to question 5</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p02-06"><h3>Question 6: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Ask successful traders whether they remember using the ritual. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Selection and retrospective recall bias the comparison.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare confidence before and after performing the ritual. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Confidence can change without forecast accuracy changing.</dd>
<dt>C. Randomly assign ritual and no-ritual trials, then score all forecasts. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Randomization and complete prospective scoring separate the ritual from selected successes.</dd>
<dt>D. Compare voluntary ritual users with people who decline it. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Self-selection may explain performance differences.</dd>
<dt>E. Compare forecasts before and after the ritual began. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Changes in task difficulty or experience can confound the comparison.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.html">Chapter 8</a> · <a href="../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.html">Chapter 15</a>. <a href="#p02-06">Back to question 6</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="2" data-question="p02-07"><h3>Question 7: C</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. The test&#x27;s sensitivity as the probability of success after passing. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This reverses the relevant conditional.</dd>
<dt>B. Equal prior probabilities because the applicant is unfamiliar. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Unfamiliarity does not imply a 50–50 base rate.</dd>
<dt>C. A justified novice reference class and test performance relevant to that class. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Resemblance alone cannot supply the prior or justify transporting the likelihoods.</dd>
<dt>D. The number of favorable adjectives in the applicant&#x27;s description. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Descriptive detail does not determine diagnostic evidence.</dd>
<dt>E. The engineer base rate because the applicant matches the prototype. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Resemblance does not establish membership in the validated population.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/09-availability-affect-and-representativeness.html">Chapter 9</a> · <a href="../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.html">Chapter 14</a>. <a href="#p02-07">Back to question 7</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p02-08"><h3>Question 8: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Attribute every gain after coaching to the intervention. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Temporal order alone does not isolate the causal contribution.</dd>
<dt>B. Compare only each coached branch with its own worst month. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This retains the selection-on-extremes problem.</dd>
<dt>C. Compare coached low scorers with the highest-scoring branches. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Different initial selection creates different regression tendencies.</dd>
<dt>D. Ask coaches to select only branches that later improved. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Selection on outcomes biases the assessment.</dd>
<dt>E. Randomly assign similarly low-scoring branches to coaching or control. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Both groups are selected on low scores, separating treatment from expected regression.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/10-confirmation-bias-and-motivated-reasoning.html">Chapter 10</a> · <a href="../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.html">Chapter 15</a>. <a href="#p02-08">Back to question 8</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="4" data-question="p02-09"><h3>Question 9: E</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. 80% success and 20% failure <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>These are individual-component rates.</dd>
<dt>B. 64% success and 36% failure <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>This treats success as requiring both components to work.</dd>
<dt>C. 40% success and 60% failure <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>These do not follow from either the rule or independence.</dd>
<dt>D. 100% success and 0% failure <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>Independent redundancy reduces failure without eliminating it.</dd>
<dt>E. 96% success and 4% failure <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Failure requires both components to fail: 0.2×0.2 = 0.04.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/12-framing.html">Chapter 12</a> · <a href="../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.html">Chapter 14</a>. <a href="#p02-09">Back to question 9</a></p></li>
<li data-answer="3" data-question="p02-10"><h3>Question 10: D</h3><p class="practice-your-answer" hidden></p><dl>
<dt>A. Both are calibrated; B has greater resolution. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>B assigns a constant probability and does not distinguish risk groups.</dd>
<dt>B. Only B is calibrated; A has greater resolution. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>A&#x27;s two forecast bins each match their outcome frequency.</dd>
<dt>C. Neither is calibrated; both have equal resolution. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>The observed frequencies match both sets of stated probabilities.</dd>
<dt>D. Both are calibrated on this record; A has greater resolution. <span class="practice-verdict">(Correct)</span></dt><dd>Both match frequencies at their stated probabilities, while A separates lower- from higher-frequency groups.</dd>
<dt>E. Only A is calibrated; both have equal resolution. <span class="practice-verdict">(Incorrect)</span></dt><dd>B&#x27;s 50% equals the overall 100/200 frequency, and A separates risks better.</dd>
</dl><p class="practice-source">Review: <a href="../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.html">Chapter 8</a> · <a href="../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.html">Chapter 15</a>. <a href="#p02-10">Back to question 10</a></p></li>
</ol></details></form>

::: {.content-visible when-format="epub"}
Choose one answer (A–E) for each of the 10 questions. Record all your choices before following the link to the answer key. Each question is worth one point.

::: {#p02-01 .practice-question}
**Question 1.** An estimate starts near an arbitrary number supplied by an interviewer. Separately, a risk estimate rises because a dramatic example comes easily to mind. Which pair fits, in order?

A) Availability; anchoring
B) Anchoring; availability
C) Priming; regression to the mean
D) Halo; conjunction fallacy
E) Framing; overplacement

:::

::: {#p02-02 .practice-question}
**Question 2.** A report changes “8% failures” to “92% successes” for the same binary outcome. Another task presents cooking words before an ambiguous word. Which processes are manipulated, respectively?

A) Defaults and anchoring
B) Semantic priming and framing
C) Framing and semantic priming
D) Loss aversion and overprecision
E) Mere exposure and a conjunction error

:::

::: {#p02-03 .practice-question}
**Question 3.** A policy slogan claiming that a reform cuts waiting times is easy to process and repeated often. Its supporters accept it without checking the evidence. Which procedure most directly tests its accuracy?

A) State a falsifiable prediction and examine independent outcome data.
B) Compare how much the two sides like their slogans.
C) Use a harder font to make the slogan feel less familiar.
D) Ask supporters how natural it sounds.
E) Repeat it to a larger group and count recognition.

:::

::: {#p02-04 .practice-question}
**Question 4.** A recruitment panel wants to prevent an engaging interview from dominating unrelated skill judgments. Which scoring procedure best targets this problem?

A) Average repeated overall-impression ratings collected during the same interview.
B) Give each interviewer an equal vote on the candidate's overall impression.
C) Require a longer explanation of the overall impression before scoring dimensions.
D) Rate job-relevant dimensions separately before recording an overall impression.
E) Record an overall impression first and use it to guide dimension ratings.

:::

::: {#p02-05 .practice-question}
**Question 5.** Every application has a final outcome recorded as either success or failure. A report says 3% fail. Its complementary frame must describe the same applications and period. Which statement qualifies?

A) 3% of accepted applicants later fail.
B) 97% of those applications succeed.
C) 97 applications succeed.
D) 3% fewer applications fail than last year.
E) 97% of rejected applicants would succeed elsewhere.

:::

::: {#p02-06 .practice-question}
**Question 6.** A trader says a new ritual improves forecasting accuracy. Which test most directly estimates its causal effect on comparable forecasting tasks?

A) Ask successful traders whether they remember using the ritual.
B) Compare confidence before and after performing the ritual.
C) Randomly assign ritual and no-ritual trials, then score all forecasts.
D) Compare voluntary ritual users with people who decline it.
E) Compare forecasts before and after the ritual began.

:::

::: {#p02-07 .practice-question}
**Question 7.** An applicant resembles a successful engineer. A selection test was validated on experienced engineers, but the current applicant pool consists of novices with a different base rate. What should a probability estimate use?

A) The test's sensitivity as the probability of success after passing.
B) Equal prior probabilities because the applicant is unfamiliar.
C) A justified novice reference class and test performance relevant to that class.
D) The number of favorable adjectives in the applicant's description.
E) The engineer base rate because the applicant matches the prototype.

:::

::: {#p02-08 .practice-question}
**Question 8.** The lowest-scoring branches receive coaching and improve next month. Which comparison best tests whether coaching contributed beyond regression to the mean?

A) Attribute every gain after coaching to the intervention.
B) Compare only each coached branch with its own worst month.
C) Compare coached low scorers with the highest-scoring branches.
D) Ask coaches to select only branches that later improved.
E) Randomly assign similarly low-scoring branches to coaching or control.

:::

::: {#p02-09 .practice-question}
**Question 9.** A project succeeds if at least one of two independent components works. Each component works with probability 0.8. Which pair gives equivalent success and failure descriptions for the project?

A) 80% success and 20% failure
B) 64% success and 36% failure
C) 40% success and 60% failure
D) 100% success and 0% failure
E) 96% success and 4% failure

:::

::: {#p02-10 .practice-question}
**Question 10.** Across 200 resolved events, A assigned 20% to 100 events, of which 20 occurred, and 80% to 100 events, of which 80 occurred. B assigned 50% to all 200. What does this record show?

A) Both are calibrated; B has greater resolution.
B) Only B is calibrated; A has greater resolution.
C) Neither is calibrated; both have equal resolution.
D) Both are calibrated on this record; A has greater resolution.
E) Only A is calibrated; both have equal resolution.

:::

[Finished the set? Check the answers and explanations.](#answers-p02)

::: {#answers-p02 .practice-answer-key}
**Answers and explanations**

Count one point for each correct answer, then review the explanations for any alternatives you considered.

**Question 1: B.**

- **A. Availability; anchoring (Incorrect)** This reverses the mechanisms.
- **B. Anchoring; availability (Correct)** The first uses a numerical starting point; the second uses ease of recall.
- **C. Priming; regression to the mean (Incorrect)** The second is not a repeated extreme measurement.
- **D. Halo; conjunction fallacy (Incorrect)** Neither a global impression nor a probability conjunction is described.
- **E. Framing; overplacement (Incorrect)** No equivalent descriptions or ranking of personal ability is specified.

Review: [Chapter 9](../chapters/09-availability-affect-and-representativeness.qmd) · [Chapter 11](../chapters/11-anchors-halos-and-decoys.qmd). [Back to question 1](#p02-01).

**Question 2: C.**

- **A. Defaults and anchoring (Incorrect)** No preselected option or initial numerical estimate is manipulated.
- **B. Semantic priming and framing (Incorrect)** This reverses the described manipulations.
- **C. Framing and semantic priming (Correct)** The first changes equivalent description; the second changes concept accessibility.
- **D. Loss aversion and overprecision (Incorrect)** Neither outcome demonstrates these particular judgment patterns.
- **E. Mere exposure and a conjunction error (Incorrect)** Repetition-based liking and intersecting probabilities are not the tasks.

Review: [Chapter 12](../chapters/12-framing.qmd) · [Chapter 13](../chapters/13-priming-fluency-and-familiarity.qmd). [Back to question 2](#p02-02).

**Question 3: A.**

- **A. State a falsifiable prediction and examine independent outcome data. (Correct)** This replaces fluency and repetition with an evidential test.
- **B. Compare how much the two sides like their slogans. (Incorrect)** Liking is not a test of the claim.
- **C. Use a harder font to make the slogan feel less familiar. (Incorrect)** Lower fluency does not itself establish falsity or truth.
- **D. Ask supporters how natural it sounds. (Incorrect)** Naturalness is another fluency judgment.
- **E. Repeat it to a larger group and count recognition. (Incorrect)** Recognition measures exposure, not accuracy.

Review: [Chapter 10](../chapters/10-confirmation-bias-and-motivated-reasoning.qmd) · [Chapter 13](../chapters/13-priming-fluency-and-familiarity.qmd). [Back to question 3](#p02-03).

**Question 4: D.**

- **A. Average repeated overall-impression ratings collected during the same interview. (Incorrect)** Averaging global ratings does not isolate evidence for distinct skills.
- **B. Give each interviewer an equal vote on the candidate's overall impression. (Incorrect)** Equal voting weights do not address each evaluator's halo effect.
- **C. Require a longer explanation of the overall impression before scoring dimensions. (Incorrect)** Elaborating the impression may reinforce rather than separate it.
- **D. Rate job-relevant dimensions separately before recording an overall impression. (Correct)** Separate initial ratings constrain spillover from a global evaluation.
- **E. Record an overall impression first and use it to guide dimension ratings. (Incorrect)** The global judgment may shape each later assessment.

Review: [Chapter 8](../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.qmd) · [Chapter 11](../chapters/11-anchors-halos-and-decoys.qmd). [Back to question 4](#p02-04).

**Question 5: B.**

- **A. 3% of accepted applicants later fail. (Incorrect)** This uses a new conditional denominator and outcome.
- **B. 97% of those applications succeed. (Correct)** Success complements failure within the specified population.
- **C. 97 applications succeed. (Incorrect)** A count needs the total number of applications to express the same rate.
- **D. 3% fewer applications fail than last year. (Incorrect)** This introduces a comparison over time absent from the original.
- **E. 97% of rejected applicants would succeed elsewhere. (Incorrect)** This changes both the population and the outcome.

Review: [Chapter 12](../chapters/12-framing.qmd) · [Chapter 14](../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.qmd). [Back to question 5](#p02-05).

**Question 6: C.**

- **A. Ask successful traders whether they remember using the ritual. (Incorrect)** Selection and retrospective recall bias the comparison.
- **B. Compare confidence before and after performing the ritual. (Incorrect)** Confidence can change without forecast accuracy changing.
- **C. Randomly assign ritual and no-ritual trials, then score all forecasts. (Correct)** Randomization and complete prospective scoring separate the ritual from selected successes.
- **D. Compare voluntary ritual users with people who decline it. (Incorrect)** Self-selection may explain performance differences.
- **E. Compare forecasts before and after the ritual began. (Incorrect)** Changes in task difficulty or experience can confound the comparison.

Review: [Chapter 8](../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.qmd) · [Chapter 15](../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.qmd). [Back to question 6](#p02-06).

**Question 7: C.**

- **A. The test's sensitivity as the probability of success after passing. (Incorrect)** This reverses the relevant conditional.
- **B. Equal prior probabilities because the applicant is unfamiliar. (Incorrect)** Unfamiliarity does not imply a 50–50 base rate.
- **C. A justified novice reference class and test performance relevant to that class. (Correct)** Resemblance alone cannot supply the prior or justify transporting the likelihoods.
- **D. The number of favorable adjectives in the applicant's description. (Incorrect)** Descriptive detail does not determine diagnostic evidence.
- **E. The engineer base rate because the applicant matches the prototype. (Incorrect)** Resemblance does not establish membership in the validated population.

Review: [Chapter 9](../chapters/09-availability-affect-and-representativeness.qmd) · [Chapter 14](../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.qmd). [Back to question 7](#p02-07).

**Question 8: E.**

- **A. Attribute every gain after coaching to the intervention. (Incorrect)** Temporal order alone does not isolate the causal contribution.
- **B. Compare only each coached branch with its own worst month. (Incorrect)** This retains the selection-on-extremes problem.
- **C. Compare coached low scorers with the highest-scoring branches. (Incorrect)** Different initial selection creates different regression tendencies.
- **D. Ask coaches to select only branches that later improved. (Incorrect)** Selection on outcomes biases the assessment.
- **E. Randomly assign similarly low-scoring branches to coaching or control. (Correct)** Both groups are selected on low scores, separating treatment from expected regression.

Review: [Chapter 10](../chapters/10-confirmation-bias-and-motivated-reasoning.qmd) · [Chapter 15](../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.qmd). [Back to question 8](#p02-08).

**Question 9: E.**

- **A. 80% success and 20% failure (Incorrect)** These are individual-component rates.
- **B. 64% success and 36% failure (Incorrect)** This treats success as requiring both components to work.
- **C. 40% success and 60% failure (Incorrect)** These do not follow from either the rule or independence.
- **D. 100% success and 0% failure (Incorrect)** Independent redundancy reduces failure without eliminating it.
- **E. 96% success and 4% failure (Correct)** Failure requires both components to fail: 0.2×0.2 = 0.04.

Review: [Chapter 12](../chapters/12-framing.qmd) · [Chapter 14](../chapters/14-base-rates-and-bayesian-updating.qmd). [Back to question 9](#p02-09).

**Question 10: D.**

- **A. Both are calibrated; B has greater resolution. (Incorrect)** B assigns a constant probability and does not distinguish risk groups.
- **B. Only B is calibrated; A has greater resolution. (Incorrect)** A's two forecast bins each match their outcome frequency.
- **C. Neither is calibrated; both have equal resolution. (Incorrect)** The observed frequencies match both sets of stated probabilities.
- **D. Both are calibrated on this record; A has greater resolution. (Correct)** Both match frequencies at their stated probabilities, while A separates lower- from higher-frequency groups.
- **E. Only A is calibrated; both have equal resolution. (Incorrect)** B's 50% equals the overall 100/200 frequency, and A separates risks better.

Review: [Chapter 8](../chapters/08-intuition-and-deliberation.qmd) · [Chapter 15](../chapters/15-randomness-and-overconfidence.qmd). [Back to question 10](#p02-10).

:::
